text: Yoido Full Gospel Church (Korean: 여의도 순복음 교회) is a Pentecostal church affiliated with the Assemblies of God located on Yeouido (Yoi Island) in Seoul, South Korea. With approximately 870,000 members, it is the largest Pentecostal Christian congregation in South Korea. Founded in 1958 by Pastor David Yonggi Cho and his mother-in-law, Choi Ja-shil, both Assemblies of God pastors, the church began with a worship service on 15 May 1958 in Choi Ja-shil's home, attended by her three daughters, one of whom later married David Yonggi Cho, and one elderly woman who came to escape the rain. The two pastors launched a campaign of door-to-door outreach, offering spiritual and humanitarian aid, and praying for the sick. Within months, membership reached fifty, prompting the move to a tent in Choi Ja-shil's backyard. As the church grew, it outgrew each tent. Pastor Cho introduced the concept of the Three-Fold Blessing—spirit, soul, and body—asserting that physical health and financial prosperity are part of God's will for Christians, which attracted many new members, bringing the total to one thousand by early 1961. The church purchased land in Seodaemun to accommodate its growth. When Cho was called for mandatory military service, he was assigned to an American Army base near Seoul, where he continued preaching with the help of missionary John Hurston. Due to illness, he was discharged and still pastored the church. On 15 October 1961, the inaugural service was held in the newly built Full Gospel Revival Center on the Seodaemun land. Membership grew to three thousand by 1964 and eight thousand by 1968. In 1967, Cho restructured the church by dividing Seoul into zones, creating "cells" where members met weekly in homes led by "cell leaders" for worship and Bible study. Women were appointed as cell leaders, a decision that challenged traditional Korean cultural norms, but the cell system proved highly successful, expanding from 125 cells in 1967 to several thousand by 2015. In 1960, a Women's Fellowship was established, followed by a Men's Fellowship in 1963, enabling lay members to serve in various volunteer roles. Membership reached ten thousand in the early 1970s. After outgrowing its Seodaemun site, the church sought a new location. Cho and leaders decided to buy land on Yeouido, directly across from Korea's National Assembly, believing they had heard from God. Construction was delayed by economic difficulties, including the 1973 oil shock, but the new auditorium was completed in 1973 and opened on 19 August with a service for 12,000 attendees. A month later, Full Gospel Central Church hosted the 10th Pentecostal World Conference at Hyochang Stadium. Membership reached fifty thousand by 1977, doubling in two years, with a special service celebrating the milestone featuring Demos Shakarian as guest speaker. Beginning in the 1980s, the church established satellite locations throughout Seoul and beyond due to physical expansion limits. Despite the auditorium being expanded to seat 12,000 in 1983, seven Sunday services were insufficient. In 1993, with 700,000 members, the church was recognized as the world's largest congregation by the Guinness Book of World Records. Despite member drain to satellite churches, new recruits through the cell network maintained membership at 780,000 in 2003. The church was renamed Yoido Full Gospel Church in the 1990s. David Yonggi Cho retired multiple times, but infighting among ministers prompted him to return from retirement, most recently in late 2006. As of 2007, membership stood at 830,000, with seven Sunday services translated into 16 languages. On 9 January 2009, a Sunday service was featured in a BBC documentary, *Around the World in 80 Faiths*. In 2008, Young Hoon Lee became senior pastor. In 2025, the church had 480,000 people in Seoul. The church has established numerous ministries for local and international outreach. It has sent missionaries to 63 countries, establishing 1,218 churches and guiding over 140,000 people in faith, beginning overseas missions in 1964 with Pastor Cho Yong-gi's work in the United States. On 20 August 2012, a pastor from the church, Seong, was caught on CCTV urinating in the Dharma hall of Donghwasa Temple and vandalizing Buddhist portraits with a permanent marker. In November 2013, the Church Reform Prayer Meeting revealed allegations that David Yonggi Cho had given 1.5 billion won to Jeong Gwi-sun, author of *Butterfly Lady of Paris*, as hush money. Despite forming a Church Investigation Committee, the inquiry did not address the affair. Jeong Gwi-sun, identified as the alleged mistress, supported Cho and claimed in January 2014 that the book was fictional and unrelated to Cho, and sued six elders from the prayer meeting. On 14 February 2014, she publicly apologized to the church, Rev. Cho, and its members. On 20 February 2014, Pastor Cho and his son Hee-jun were convicted of embezzling US$12 million in church funds. A presiding judge told Cho, "We know that this case is not your problem. You just need to blame it on your son, then you will have no responsibilities," to which Cho responded, "My son can be unrighteous to me, but I cannot be unrighteous to my son." The case was dismissed in June 2016 due to "no suspicion." In May 2023, Young Hoon Lee sparked controversy by attending the opening ceremony of the Liberty Korea Party's headquarters in Yeongdeungpo-gu, Seoul, where he urged attendees to support Jeon Kwang-hoon in his call to "eradicate communist reds," a phrase now considered outdated propaganda. The incident intensified because Jeon previously made statements like "God, Freeze!" seen as blasphemous, and has been labeled a "heretic" by mainstream Protestant groups in South Korea. The event drew criticism as it appeared the leader of South Korea's largest church was publicly endorsing a figure condemned by many in the Christian community.
